title: Elastic Harmony Scheduler: token vs request equity (sketch)
body:
Purpose and context:
This is a working sketch for a continuous, low-latency scheduler that reconciles two common design axes: token-level packing (maximizes throughput by filling kernel batches with tokens) and request-level fairness (preserves per-request latency and SLA equity). Many of our existing sketches treat these as separate designs. Elastic Harmony aims to merge them into a single adaptive strategy that: (1) respects request-level latency SLOs and fairness constraints, (2) opportunistically packs tokens to improve utilization, and (3) honors kernel and KV-cache affinities to avoid regressing end-to-end tail latency.

Why we need another sketch (short):
- Observed: heavy token packing increases utilization but sharply penalizes short, latency-sensitive requests (micro-requests) and those with cold KV caches.
- Observed: strict request-level scheduling preserves latency but wastes GPU cycles for many small requests.
- Goal: a pragmatic policy that can be rolled out incrementally (canaryable), instrumented, and tuned per-customer/route.

High-level idea: per-request equity credit + token opportunism
- Each incoming request r arrives with metadata: request_id, qos_priority, max_latency_slo_ms, sequence_length_estimate, kv_prefix_key (optional), kernel_hint (optional).
- Maintain two related queues: RequestQueue (RQ) and TokenWindow (TW). RQ holds request-level descriptors and outstanding token counts; TW is the short-lived packing window used to assemble tokens into a kernel-friendly micro-batch.
- Each request carries an \"equity credit\" E_r. Equity credits are consumed when the request waits (accumulates) or when it is chosen to be served late relative to its SLO. The scheduler aims to equalize normalized served fraction over a sliding horizon using credits (inspired by deficit round-robin but continuous and token-aware).

Core policy loop (conceptual):
1) Admission: when request arrives, allocate initial E_r proportional to qos_priority and inverse to sequence_length_estimate (short requests get small boost).
2) Candidate selection: periodically (every 1–3ms), assemble a TW by pulling from RQ ordered by (deficit/E_r, slack_to_slo) heuristics — this biases toward requests with low served fraction and those approaching latency limit.
3) Kernel packing: inside TW, we perform token-level packing up to a target micro-batch token budget (T_target) that changes with observed latency and GPU backpressure.
4) Kernel compatibility check: for the assembled micro-batch, compute kernel compatibility vector (quantized-ops, kv-affinity, kv-cache-hit-prob). If compatibility is poor, either split TW or defer low-affinity requests to the next window (soft fallback).
5) Dispatch: launch kernel; on completion, update each request's served tokens, E_r, and per-request latency accounting.
6) Rebalance credits: if a request exceeds its latency SLO, compensate by increasing E_r for similar class requests for a short epoch to reduce their waiting.

Why this is different than naive token-level packing:
- Naive: greedily fill tokens => best throughput but starvation for some requests.
- Elastic Harmony: uses per-request equity credits + slack-to-slo to bias selection and still packs tokens opportunistically, but includes kernel compatibility heuristics to reduce worst-case tail amplifications (e.g., mixing long KV-unfriendly requests into a packed kernel).

Data structures (sketch):
- RQ: priority queue keyed by score(r) = deficit(r) / (1 + log(1 + wait_ms)) * class_factor. Stored as an index pointing to request descriptor objects.
- Request descriptor: {request_id, arrival_ts, seq_est, tokens_outstanding, E_r, qos_priority, kv_key_hint, kernel_hint, last_dispatched_ts}. (In implementation this is a flat struct placed in ring-buffer memory for cache locality.)
- TW: small vector of request_refs + per-slot token allocation; ephemeral and discarded after dispatch.

Deficit / equity semantics (informal):
- We track for each request class C a notion of fair share over window W: ideal_tokens_C = total_tokens_served_in_W * weight_C. Each class maintains a deficit counter D_C = ideal_tokens_C - tokens_served_C. Requests inherit class-level deficit shaping and consume from it (so individual short request variance is smoothed).
- For strict per-request fairness (enterprise tenant opt-in), we can assign each request its own weight and run the same logic at per-tenant granularity.

Kernel compatibility and KV cache affinity:
- We collect simple telemetry: per-request kv_prefix -> last_cache_hit_ts; kernel_hint provided by model compiler (e.g., attention pattern, fused_kernel_id).
- When building TW, prefer grouping requests that share kernel_hint and have similar kv_cache_hit probability. Adding heterogeneous requests reduces vectorization and may increase memcopies, so we add a penalty term to selection score for dissimilarities.
- If penalty exceeds threshold, split TW into two smaller dispatches (cost model compares extra kernel launch overhead vs expected token throughput loss).

Adaptive T_target and backpressure:
- T_target is adjusted by an inner control loop to maintain P50 service latency under target. If P99 increases, T_target decays faster. If utilization low and P50 well under target, T_target increases. This keeps the scheduler responsive to burstiness.

Pseudocode (high-level):
-- main loop (every 2ms):
  collect metrics
  adjust T_target
  TW = []
  while TW.tokens < T_target and RQ not empty:
    r = pop_best_request(RQ) // uses score combining E_r and slack_to_slo
    allocate = min(r.tokens_outstanding, T_target - TW.tokens)
    TW.append({r, allocate})
    r.tokens_outstanding -= allocate
    if r.tokens_outstanding > 0: reinsert r into RQ with updated score
  if kernel_compatibility(TW) < threshold: split_or_defer(TW)
  dispatch(TW)
  on completion: update E_r, per-request latency, kv-cache stats, token counters

Instrumentation and SLOs to track:
- per-request: request_latency_ms, tokens_served, kernel_hint, kv_cache_hit (bool)
- aggregated: GPU_utilization, average_micro_batch_tokens, kernel_launch_rate, TW_split_rate, Jain_fairness_index over per-request served fraction, P50/P95/P99 latencies by request class, kv_cache_hit_rate, bytes_copied_for_batching
- alerts: rise in TW_split_rate or kernel_compatibility penalty (indicates kernel fragmentation), Jain index below threshold, per-tenant P99 > SLA

Experiment matrix (initial canary):
- baseline: current token-first continuous batcher (A)
- policy-1: Elastic Harmony with light equity bias (fast packing; E_r small)
- policy-2: Elastic Harmony with strong fairness (E_r large)
- policy-3: policy-2 + kernel_compatibility penalty enabled
Metrics to compare: throughput @ P50, P95, P99 latencies for short (<64 tokens) vs long (>512 tokens) requests; throughput per-GPU, KV cache-hit sensitivity test (synthetic probes that flip cache locality).

Rollout & safety knobs:
- route-level knobs: per-route fairness_mode in {throughput-first, balanced, strict-fair}
- global emergency: max_microbatch_tokens hard cap; fall-back to request-level FIFO if P99 exceeds emergency threshold for sustained window
- gradual % traffic canary with metric guardrails (P95 increase > 10% => rollback)

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
1) Equity credit shaping: should credits be per-request or per-tenant? Per-tenant smooths variance but hides bad actor requests. Proposal: per-tenant by default, per-request optional for strict SLO customers.
2) Cost model accuracy: the decision to split TW vs accept heterogeneity depends on a cost model comparing extra kernel launch overhead to degraded throughput. We need microbenchmarks across kernels (fused attention variants, quantized vs fp16) — schedule a benchmarking run.
3) KV cache interaction: mixing cold-prefix requests with hot-prefix ones may reduce overall cache hit rate. Should we prioritize cache-hot requests into hot windows? Early heuristics suggest yes, but we must measure end-to-end latency win/loss.
4) Implementation complexity: can we implement RQ as a single lock-free priority queue without regressing enqueue latency at high concurrency? If not, consider sharded RQs per-core and a small global rebalancer.
5) What is the right rhythm for the micro-window (1ms, 2ms, 5ms)? Lower gives lower latency but hurts packing. We will sweep in experiments.

Short TODOs (next steps):
- [ ] Add microbench harness that simulates mixed short/long request traces + KV hot/cold mix (owner: Daniel)
- [ ] Implement kernel_compatibility scorer prototype in C++ runtime (owner: Priya)
- [ ] Telemetry plan: add TW_split_rate and kernel_hint tagging to spans (owner: Liam)
- [ ] Draft route-level config and console toggles for fairness_mode (owner: product:console-team)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic and hybrid. Treat this as a prototype for a family of policies; we should prefer small, observable changes for canary rollouts.
- If we accept per-tenant credit defaults, we must provide an escape hatch for tenants who want strict per-request SLAs.

References and inspiration:
- deficit round-robin and weighted fair queueing literature (simplified here)
- prior Redwood sketches on continuous coalescing (see linked PR and Slack thread)
- internal microbench results: /bench/packing/2024-10 (ask infra for latest CSV)

Unresolved design note (one-liner):
- consider factoring kernel_compatibility into model compilation phase so runtime only inspects a compact affinity tag (cheap) rather than measuring heavy signals at scheduling time.

End of sketch.

Choppy notes / scratch ideas (keep local):
- Could use exponential backoff on low-priority requests that frequently cause splits — reduces fragmentation over time.
- Maybe expose a hint to customers: prefer_throughput vs prefer_latency to let user set E_r bias at API call-level.
- Consider a fast-path for single-token responses: a bypass that always dispatches immediately if predicted cost < X microsecs (only for enterprise customers who opt in).
